title: Effectiveness of Curriculum Learning Depends on Reward Sparsity and Competing Optima
claim: A minimal interception task with stochastic actions and dense versus sparse returns shows why uninformative rewards make curricula necessary.
layout: Single horizontal strip of small schematics, left-to-right, with math annotations
description: A wide, short strip of small schematic panels that appears cropped at the top. On the left, rows of episodes show a blue square (agent action) and a red bullseye (target) on horizontal arrows labelled 'action', with the equation u-bar = b + w^T z_t above. Next is a blue diamond labelled 'exploration / policy noise', the Gaussian sampling formula u_t ~ N(u-bar, 1/beta_t), and a blue bell curve over u. To the right is a green return curve G versus u, labelled 'sparse', with a narrow spike at the target u_R. Next to it is a 'uninformative reward' arrow diagram with a green zone around the target. At far right are magenta Sigma_t decay curves over time, marked 'increasing task difficulty'. Colour carries meaning: blue for the agent, red for the target, green for return, magenta for curriculum.
caption: Schematic of task and curriculum learning problem. a) During episode $t$, the agent receives an $F$-dimensional state vector $\vec{z}_t$ as input and must generate a scalar action $u_t$. The goal of the task is to have $u_t$ match a target action $u_R$. b) Learning dynamics are stochastic because of feature variance and policy noise. c) We consider two types of returns: a quadratic dense return, and a sparse return that equals a quadratic plus a Gaussian bump. The latter often provides uninformative reward signals if the Gaussian is sufficiently narrow. d) Specifying a curriculum means specifying how some combination of $\beta_t$ and $\vec{\Sigma}_t$ change over training. abstract: While animals and people tend to learn a task more quickly and reliably when they first train on simpler versions of it, curriculum learning's effectiveness in artificial settings varies, and appears substantially greater in reinforcement learning than in supervised learning. In this work, we construct and analyze a minimal model of policy learning to better understand why. We consider an open-loop, episodic target interception task whose parameters---especially how close the agent must be to the target to receive an informative reward signal---can be chosen so that the agent either receives informative rewards frequently ('dense' rewards) or rarely ('sparse' rewards). We mathematically and numerically analyze the dynamics of REINFORCE-based policy learning in both cases. In the dense reward case, curricula have only marginal benefits; in the sparse case, curricula can be required for learning to occur at all. We find that this is especially true when the agent has the conflicting goals of minimizing effort and accumulating high reward, since this can produce distinct reward landscape optima which compete with one another. Our characterization of useful curricula in this setting indicates that they address two issues: they (i) make rewards less sparse to speed up learning, and (ii) shape the reward landscape to steer agents away from bad local optima.
